voiceover_script: 47 customers quietly stopped ordering last month. You didn't notice. You were too busy processing refunds. But those 47 customers? That's $12,000 in annual LTV you just lost. And you don't even know their names.

Everyone thinks refund fraud is your biggest problem. It's not even close. Silent churn costs 10x more. A customer who complains twice and disappears is worth more than 100 refund disputes. But restaurants never measure it.

I've worked with 50+ restaurants. The pattern is always the same. Kitchen doesn't know customer history. Packer has zero context. Same mistake happens twice. Customer leaves for good. That's the gap everyone ignores.

Stop guessing which customers are repeat complainers. You probably don't even track it. Meanwhile, the same people are ordering again, getting the same mistake, and leaving forever. That's preventable loss.
2 mistakes. That's all it takes. 86% don't come back. But most restaurants don't even track first mistakes. They just see the refund. They never connect it to the person who stops ordering.

One notification at the packing station. That's all it takes to prevent the refund. But your packer doesn't see it. They don't know this customer complained before. So they pack it the same wrong way. Again.

I've calculated this with hundreds of restaurants. A $20 refund stings. But losing a customer worth $3,000 per year? That destroys your unit economics. Yet restaurants obsess over the refund and ignore the churn.

Everyone blames the kitchen for mistakes. Wrong angle. The real problem is your CS team and kitchen never talk. CS knows the customer is a repeat complainer. Kitchen doesn't. Information doesn't flow. That's the design flaw.

3 customers per week silently churn from your operation. You don't see it. No refund request. No complaint. Just gone. Over a year, that's 156 customers. That's six figures in lost revenue you never knew existed.
Stop managing by refund. Start managing by retention. One tells you what you lost. The other tells you who's about to leave. Restaurants do the first and ignore the second. That's backwards.
